prompt: What is a covalent bond?

choices.text: A bond formed when two atoms share electrons
The attraction between ions formed when electrons transfer
choices.why: That describes an ionic bond. In a covalent bond, electrons are shared between the atoms rather than transferred.

choices.text: A bond that forms only between two atoms of the same element
choices.why: Covalent bonds also form between different elements, as in HF. What makes a bond covalent is that the electrons are shared.

choices.text: The attraction between a nucleus and its own valence electrons
choices.why: That attraction holds an atom's own electrons; it doesn't join two atoms. A covalent bond joins two atoms by sharing electrons between them.

explanation: When electrons are shared between two atoms, they form a covalent bond. Sharing is another way, besides electron transfer, for atoms to obtain complete valence shells.

prompt: According to the section, when do atoms form a covalent bond instead of an ionic bond?

choices.text: When the atoms don't easily give up or gain electrons, so they share electrons to fill their valence shells
When one atom easily loses electrons and the other atom easily gains them
choices.why: That is when ionic bonding typically occurs: electrons transfer from one atom to the other, making ions.

choices.text: When both atoms already have complete valence shells before they meet
choices.why: Atoms bond to obtain complete valence shells. Atoms whose shells are already complete have nothing to gain by sharing.

choices.text: When both atoms start with the same number of valence electrons
choices.why: Atoms with different numbers of valence electrons also bond covalently; in HF, H has one valence electron and F has seven.

explanation: Ionic bonding typically occurs when one atom easily loses electrons and another easily gains them. Atoms that don't give up or gain electrons easily can still complete their valence shells by sharing electrons, which makes a covalent bond.

prompt: Hydrogen is one of the diatomic elements, found as H2 molecules. How does the section explain this?

choices.text: Two H atoms share their electrons, so each has two electrons and a filled 1s subshell.
One H atom transfers its electron to the other, and the two ions attract.
choices.why: A transfer would leave one H atom with no electrons. In H2 the electrons are shared, so both atoms have filled valence shells.

choices.text: Two H atoms share electrons until each has an octet of eight electrons.
choices.why: An H atom needs only two electrons to fill its 1s subshell, not eight.

choices.text: Two H atoms share two pairs of electrons, so each has four electrons.
choices.why: Each H atom has only one electron to contribute, so the atoms share one pair, which is all an H atom needs.

explanation: Each H atom starts with one electron. By sharing them, the two atoms form a single covalent bond, and each H atom has the two electrons that fill its 1s subshell. Because both valence shells are full, the bond is stable.

prompt: When a covalent bond is written as a dash, as in H–H, what does the dash stand for?

choices.text: One pair of electrons shared between the two atoms
One electron shared between the two atoms
choices.why: A single bond is a shared pair, so one dash stands for two electrons, one contributed by each H atom.

choices.text: One electron transferred from one atom to the other
choices.why: Transferring an electron makes ions and an ionic bond. The dash represents electrons that both atoms share.

choices.text: One lone pair of electrons on each of the two atoms
choices.why: Lone pairs do not take part in bonding. The dash stands for the bonding pair between the atoms.

explanation: The dash replaces the two dots of a shared electron pair. Two atoms sharing one pair of electrons are joined by a single bond.

prompt: In a Lewis electron dot diagram of a molecule, what are lone pair electrons?

choices.text: Pairs of valence electrons on an atom that do not take part in bonding
Pairs of electrons shared between two atoms to make a covalent bond
choices.why: Shared pairs are bonding pairs. Lone pairs stay on one atom and are not shared.

choices.text: Single unpaired electrons that an atom uses to make a bond
choices.why: Unpaired electrons are the ones atoms share to form bonds; once shared, they become a bonding pair, not a lone pair.

choices.text: Electrons removed from the count because the species has a positive charge
choices.why: Removed electrons don't appear in the diagram at all. Lone pairs are in the diagram; they just aren't in a bond.

explanation: A molecule's valence electrons are either bonding pairs, which make covalent bonds, or lone pairs, which belong to one atom and do not participate in bonding. In F2, for example, each F atom has one bonding pair and three lone pairs.

prompt: What does a double bond between two atoms represent?

choices.text: Two pairs of electrons shared between the same two atoms
Two electrons shared between the same two atoms
choices.why: Two electrons make one shared pair, which is a single bond. A double bond has two pairs, or four electrons.

choices.text: A central atom with single bonds to two different atoms
choices.why: That is two separate single bonds, as in H2O. A double bond is two bonding pairs between the same two atoms.

choices.text: Two lone pairs on each of the two bonded atoms
choices.why: Lone pairs do not participate in bonding, so they aren't part of any bond.

explanation: Two atoms can share more than one pair of electrons. Two bonding pairs between the same two atoms make a double bond, drawn with two lines, as in the C=O bond of formaldehyde.

prompt: Which statement about covalent bonding in molecules with more than two atoms is correct?

choices.text: Many atoms can be bonded together, but each covalent bond is between two atoms only.
A single shared pair of electrons can bond three or more atoms at once.
choices.why: Any given covalent bond is between two atoms only; a molecule with more atoms simply has more bonds.

choices.text: Only two atoms in a molecule can share electrons; the rest are held by ionic bonds.
choices.why: In H2O, the O atom shares a pair of electrons with each H atom, making two covalent bonds.

choices.text: Molecules with more than two atoms always contain at least one double bond.
choices.why: H2O has three atoms and only single bonds. A multiple bond is needed only when single bonds can't give every atom a full valence shell.

explanation: More than two atoms can participate in covalent bonding, but any one covalent bond is between two atoms. In H2O, for example, there are two covalent bonds, each between the O atom and one H atom.

prompt: A Br2 molecule has 14 valence electrons, 7 from each Br atom. Yet in its Lewis electron dot diagram, each Br atom is surrounded by an octet, which seems to call for 16 electrons. How is this possible?

choices.text: The two electrons in the bonding pair count toward the octets of both Br atoms.
One Br atom transfers an electron to the other, so both end up with eight.
choices.why: After a transfer, one atom would have eight electrons and the other only six. Sharing is what lets both atoms have octets.

choices.text: Each Br atom picks up an extra electron from its surroundings as the bond forms.
choices.why: No electrons are added to a neutral molecule; its Lewis diagram uses only the 14 valence electrons of the two atoms.

choices.text: Each Br atom needs only seven electrons once it is part of a molecule.
choices.why: A Br atom needs an octet, eight electrons, for a complete valence shell; being part of a molecule doesn't change that.

explanation: Each Br atom has three lone pairs (6 electrons) plus the shared bonding pair (2 electrons), for 8 around each. The bonding pair counts for both atoms, so 6 + 6 + 2 = 14 electrons give two octets.

prompt: Potassium cyanide, KCN, is made of K+ ions and cyanide ions, CN^−. Which statement describes the bonding in KCN?

choices.text: C and N are held by covalent bonds, and K+ and CN^− are held by ionic bonding.
All of its bonds are ionic, because KCN is made of ions.
choices.why: The atoms within a polyatomic ion such as CN^− are held together by covalent bonds; only the attraction between the ions is ionic.

choices.text: All of its bonds are covalent, because CN^− has covalent bonds.
choices.why: K+ and CN^− are oppositely charged ions, and their attraction is an ionic bond.

choices.text: K and C are held by covalent bonds, and C and N are held by ionic bonding.
choices.why: This reverses the two types: the C and N atoms of the cyanide ion share electrons, while K+ is attracted to the whole CN^− ion.

explanation: Polyatomic ions are bonded together with covalent bonds. Because they are ions, they also take part in ionic bonding with other ions, so KCN has both major types of bonding at the same time.

prompt: Which statement about vitamins and minerals agrees with the section?

choices.text: All vitamins are covalently bonded molecules, while most minerals are consumed in ionic form.
All vitamins are ionic compounds, while most minerals are consumed as covalent molecules.
choices.why: This reverses the two: vitamins are covalently bonded molecules, and most minerals are consumed as ions.

choices.text: Vitamins and minerals are both consumed mostly as free, uncombined elements.
choices.why: Vitamins are covalently bonded molecules, and most minerals are consumed in ionic form rather than as elements.

choices.text: Each vitamin is a single element, while minerals are molecules made of C, H, O, and N.
choices.why: Vitamins are molecules, and a mineral is an element the body needs other than carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, or nitrogen.

explanation: All vitamins are covalently bonded molecules, such as retinol (vitamin A) and ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Minerals are elements other than C, H, O, and N that the body needs, and most are consumed in ionic form rather than as elements or in covalent molecules.

prompt: In the formula H2O, H is written first, yet O is the central atom. What keeps an H atom from being the central atom?

choices.text: One shared pair fills an H atom's valence shell, so H bonds to only one other atom.
An H atom has no valence electrons of its own to share.
choices.why: Each H atom has one valence electron, which it shares to form a bond.

choices.text: An H atom needs eight electrons, more than its neighbors can share.
choices.why: An H atom needs only two electrons to fill its 1s subshell, not an octet.

choices.text: An H atom already has a full valence shell before it bonds.
choices.why: An H atom on its own has only one electron; it gets its second by sharing a pair with another atom.

explanation: A central atom bonds to two or more surrounding atoms. An H atom needs only two electrons, which one shared pair provides, so it makes just one bond. In H2O, the O atom bonds to both H atoms and is the central atom.

prompt: In the section's steps for drawing a Lewis electron dot diagram, what comes right after placing a pair of electrons between the central atom and each surrounding atom?

choices.text: Complete the octets around the surrounding atoms.
Check that every atom has a full valence shell.
choices.why: That is the last step, done only after all the valence electrons have been placed.

choices.text: Count the total number of valence electrons.
choices.why: That is step 1, done before any electrons are placed.

choices.text: Make a double bond between the central atom and each surrounding atom.
choices.why: Multiple bonds are used only if, after the steps, an atom still lacks a full valence shell.

explanation: The steps are: count the valence electrons; write the central atom surrounded by the other atoms; put a pair of electrons between the central atom and each surrounding atom; complete the octets of the surrounding atoms (except H); put any remaining electrons on the central atom; and check that every atom has a full valence shell.

prompt: How many valence electrons in total must be shown in the Lewis electron dot diagram of methanol, CH3OH?
explanation: C has 4 valence electrons, each of the four H atoms has 1, and O has 6: 4 + 4(1) + 6 = 14 valence electrons.

prompt: How many valence electrons must be accounted for in the Lewis electron dot diagram of the sulfate ion, SO4^2−?
explanation: S has 6 valence electrons and each of the four O atoms has 6, giving 6 + 4(6) = 30. The 2− charge adds two more electrons: 30 + 2 = 32.

prompt: A student counting the valence electrons for the ammonium ion, NH4^+, writes 5 + 4 × 1 + 1 = 10. What is the mistake?

choices.text: A positive charge means an electron is removed, so the total is 5 + 4 − 1 = 8.
Each H should count as 2 electrons, since H needs two: 5 + 8 + 1 = 14.
choices.why: Step 1 counts the valence electrons each atom has, and an H atom has only 1; how many it needs doesn't enter the count.

choices.text: The charge should be left out, since only atoms supply electrons: 5 + 4 = 9.
choices.why: Step 1 adjusts the count for charge: remove one electron for each positive charge and add one for each negative charge.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; a 1+ charge adds one electron, giving 10.
choices.why: A positive charge means the species has lost an electron, so one is subtracted, not added.

explanation: N has 5 valence electrons and each H has 1, for 9. The 1+ charge means one electron has been removed, so NH4^+ has 9 − 1 = 8 valence electrons.

prompt: A student follows the section's steps for nitrogen trifluoride, NF3, with N as the central atom. After step 3, in which a pair of electrons is placed between the central atom and each surrounding atom, how many valence electrons remain to be placed?
explanation: NF3 has 5 + 3(7) = 26 valence electrons. Three bonding pairs, one to each F atom, use 3 × 2 = 6 electrons, leaving 26 − 6 = 20.

prompt: When the section's steps are followed for oxygen difluoride, OF2, with O as the central atom, how many electrons are placed on the central O atom in step 5?
explanation: OF2 has 6 + 2(7) = 20 valence electrons. The two O–F bonding pairs use 4, leaving 16; completing the octets of the two F atoms uses 2 × 6 = 12, leaving 4. These 4 electrons go on the O atom as two lone pairs, giving it an octet.

prompt: In the Lewis electron dot diagram of carbon tetrachloride, CCl4, how many lone pairs of electrons are there in the whole molecule?
explanation: CCl4 has 4 + 4(7) = 32 valence electrons. Four C–Cl bonding pairs use 8, and the other 24 complete the octets of the four Cl atoms as 3 lone pairs each. The C atom has its octet from four bonds and no lone pairs, so there are 4 × 3 = 12 lone pairs.

prompt: The amide ion, NH2^−, has N as its central atom. In its Lewis electron dot diagram, how many lone pairs of electrons are on the N atom?
explanation: NH2^− has 5 + 2(1) + 1 = 8 valence electrons, including one extra for the 1− charge. Two N–H bonding pairs use 4, the H atoms need no more, and the remaining 4 go on N as 2 lone pairs, giving N an octet.

prompt: A selenium atom has six valence electrons. Each H atom can share its one electron with Se to form a covalent bond. How many H atoms must bond to a single Se atom to give it a complete octet?
explanation: Se needs 8 − 6 = 2 more electrons. Each H atom shares one electron with Se in one covalent bond, so two H atoms are needed, making H2Se. Each H atom then has the two electrons that fill its valence shell.

prompt: A student uses all 8 valence electrons of methane, CH4, to make four C–H bonding pairs. The student then says each H atom still needs six more electrons for an octet, so CH4 can't be drawn properly. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: An H atom needs only two electrons, so each H atom is already full.
CH4 really has 16 valence electrons, enough to give every H atom an octet.
choices.why: C has 4 valence electrons and each H has 1, so CH4 has 4 + 4(1) = 8.

choices.text: Each C–H bond should be a double bond to give the H atoms more electrons.
choices.why: An H atom holds only two electrons, so it forms just one single bond.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; CH4 is a molecule that cannot follow the octet rule.
choices.why: In CH4 the C atom has an octet from its four bonding pairs and each H atom has the two electrons it needs, so every atom has a full valence shell.

explanation: H atoms need only two electrons to fill their 1s subshell, which is why step 4 says to complete the octets of the surrounding atoms except for H. After step 3, each H has two electrons and the C atom has eight, so the diagram is complete.

prompt: A student drawing the Lewis electron dot diagram of phosphine, PH3, puts a pair of electrons between P and each H atom. Two valence electrons are still unused, and P has only six electrons around it, so the student turns one P–H bond into a double bond. What did the student do wrong?

choices.text: The two unused electrons belong on P as a lone pair, which gives P an octet.
PH3 has only 6 valence electrons, so no electrons should be left over.
choices.why: P has 5 valence electrons and each H has 1, so PH3 has 8; two remain after the three bonding pairs.

choices.text: The unused electrons should be discarded, because PH3 has no charge.
choices.why: Electrons are removed only for a positive charge. Every valence electron of a neutral molecule must appear in its diagram.

choices.text: Nothing; a double bond is the right fix whenever a central atom has six electrons.
choices.why: A multiple bond is considered only if an atom is still short after step 5, and an H atom can hold only two electrons, so it never forms a double bond.

explanation: PH3 has 5 + 3(1) = 8 valence electrons. Three P–H bonding pairs use 6, the H atoms need no more, and the remaining 2 go on P as a lone pair in step 5. P then has an octet, so no double bond is needed.

prompt: A student applies steps 1–5 to each of these molecules, using only single bonds. For which molecule is the central atom left short of an octet, so that double bonds are needed?

choices.text: CS2
SiH4
choices.why: SiH4's 8 valence electrons make four Si–H bonding pairs, which give Si an octet and each H two electrons.

choices.text: H2S
choices.why: H2S has 8 valence electrons: two S–H bonding pairs use 4, and the other 4 go on S as two lone pairs, giving S an octet.

choices.text: CH3Cl
choices.why: CH3Cl has 14 valence electrons: four bonding pairs use 8, the other 6 complete the Cl octet, and C already has an octet from its four bonds.

explanation: CS2 has 4 + 2(6) = 16 valence electrons. Two C–S bonding pairs use 4 and the S octets use the other 12, leaving C with only four electrons. A double bond between C and each S atom (S=C=S) gives every atom an octet.

prompt: Ethylene, C2H4, has two central C atoms bonded to each other, with two H atoms bonded to each C. Using only single bonds, its 12 valence electrons make five bonding pairs, and the last pair goes on one C atom as a lone pair. That C has an octet, but the other C has only six electrons. How should the diagram be fixed?

choices.text: Share that lone pair between the two C atoms, making a C=C double bond.
Move that lone pair over to the C atom that has only six electrons.
choices.why: Then the first C atom would have only six electrons. Moving the pair just moves the problem.

choices.text: Add a second lone pair to the C atom that has only six electrons.
choices.why: C2H4 has only 12 valence electrons, and all of them are already placed. No electrons can be added.

choices.text: Turn one C–H bond on the short C atom into a double bond.
choices.why: An H atom can hold only two electrons, so it forms only a single bond.

explanation: Two atoms can share more than one pair of electrons. Sharing the lone pair between the C atoms makes a C=C double bond; each C then has two C–H bonding pairs and two C–C bonding pairs, an octet, and all 12 valence electrons are still used.

prompt: Hydrazine, N2H4, has two central N atoms bonded to each other, and each N atom is also bonded to two H atoms. Which description of its Lewis electron dot diagram is correct?

choices.text: An N–N single bond, four N–H single bonds, and one lone pair on each N
An N=N double bond, four N–H single bonds, and no lone pairs
choices.why: This uses only 12 electrons, but N2H4 has 2(5) + 4(1) = 14. Single bonds already give each N an octet once the last 4 electrons are added as lone pairs.

choices.text: An N–N single bond, four N–H single bonds, and two lone pairs on each N
choices.why: This uses 18 electrons, 4 more than N2H4 has, and puts ten electrons around each N.

choices.text: An N≡N triple bond, four N–H single bonds, and no lone pairs
choices.why: This puts ten electrons around each N (six from the triple bond and four from the N–H bonds), more than an octet.

explanation: N2H4 has 2(5) + 4(1) = 14 valence electrons. The N–N bond and four N–H bonds use 10, and the remaining 4 go on the N atoms as one lone pair each. Each N then has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, an octet, so no multiple bond is needed.

prompt: In hydrogen cyanide, HCN, the C atom is the central atom, bonded to both H and N. Which description of its Lewis electron dot diagram is correct?

choices.text: An H–C single bond, a C≡N triple bond, and one lone pair on N
An H–C single bond, a C=N double bond, and two lone pairs on N
choices.why: This leaves C with only six electrons (two from H–C and four from C=N). C and N must share one more pair.

choices.text: An H–C single bond, a C–N single bond, and three lone pairs on N
choices.why: This is where the steps end with single bonds only, and C has just four electrons, so multiple bonding is needed.

choices.text: An H=C double bond, a C=N double bond, and one lone pair on N
choices.why: An H atom can hold only two electrons, so it forms only a single bond; this diagram also leaves N with just six electrons.

explanation: HCN has 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 valence electrons. With single bonds, the H–C and C–N pairs use 4 and N's octet uses the other 6, leaving C with only four electrons. A C≡N triple bond gives C an octet (2 + 6) and leaves N with one lone pair (6 + 2).

prompt: Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, has two central O atoms bonded to each other, and each O atom is also bonded to one H atom. How many lone pairs of electrons are there in the whole molecule's Lewis electron dot diagram?
explanation: H2O2 has 2(1) + 2(6) = 14 valence electrons. The H–O, O–O, and O–H bonding pairs use 6, leaving 8, which go on the O atoms as 2 lone pairs each. Each O then has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, an octet, for 4 lone pairs in all.

prompt: In a correct Lewis electron dot diagram of an O2 molecule, in which both O atoms have complete octets, how many lone pairs are on each O atom?
explanation: O2 has 2(6) = 12 valence electrons. A single bond would leave 10 electrons, short of the 12 needed to complete both octets, so the O atoms share two pairs in a double bond (O=O). The remaining 8 electrons form 2 lone pairs on each O, giving each 4 + 4 = 8 electrons.

prompt: In a correct Lewis electron dot diagram of the peroxide ion, O2^2−, in which both O atoms have complete octets, how many bonding pairs of electrons are shared between the two O atoms?
explanation: O2^2− has 2(6) + 2 = 14 valence electrons. One bonding pair uses 2, and the remaining 12 give each O atom 3 lone pairs, so each O has 2 + 6 = 8 electrons. Every atom already has an octet, so only a single bond is needed.

prompt: In a correct Lewis electron dot diagram of carbon monoxide, CO, in which both atoms have complete octets, how many bonding pairs of electrons are shared between the C and O atoms?
explanation: CO has 4 + 6 = 10 valence electrons. With one or two bonding pairs, too few electrons remain to complete both octets. Three bonding pairs (C≡O) use 6 electrons, and the other 4 form one lone pair on each atom, so each has 6 + 2 = 8.
